questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
questions.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
B[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

questions.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
questions.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{69} & =P{D}^{69}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{69}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{69} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{69}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
questions.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$

questions.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $B:$

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[60]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[40]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $B=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${B}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{B}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{120} & =P{D}^{120}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[60]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[40]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{120}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[60]{2})^{120} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[40]{2})^{120}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -24 \\ 12 & 32\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & 24 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
